messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Delivery Driver
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something, Authority Presence: Police, Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle, Drug Use: take drugs, Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Priya remembers the cold. It was a late November evening, four months ago, and the chill seeped through the floor of her car as she pulled up to the last delivery address of her shift. The event itself doesn't play back like a film in her mind; it exists as a series of stark, silent photographs. The first is of a man’s shape emerging from the shadows between two apartment buildings. The second is of his hand, reaching for her car door handle. The final, and most persistent, is the image of her own car’s red taillights shrinking into the darkness as he drove it away. Between these snapshots, there is mostly a blank, but her ears remember what her eyes cannot. The gruff, low command—"Get out. Phone. Keys. Now."—is a sound that can surface without warning, as clear and immediate as if the man were standing beside her. When it happens, she doesn't see his face, but she feels the same wave of cold dread, a pure, imageless emotion that leaves her breathless and trembling.

In the weeks that followed, Priya’s world began to shrink. The police had been kind, but the sight of their uniforms and the flashing lights of the cruiser now cause a knot of anxiety to tighten in her stomach. She had come to believe that their presence was not a sign of safety, but an emblem of her own failure. She would never forgive herself for her passivity during the robbery; she had simply complied, frozen, handing over everything without a fight. This inaction guilt became a constant companion, whispering that she should have done more, that she was weak. The world, in turn, felt menacing and unpredictable. She was certain she couldn't stop bad things from happening to her, so her only option was to try and anticipate them. Before entering a coffee shop or a grocery store, she would first identify all the exits, a mental checklist she had to complete before she could feel a sliver of comfort. Even at home, in her own bed, she was unable to relax, waking multiple times a night to check the locks on her doors and windows, her body perpetually braced for a threat that never materialized.

Her job as a delivery driver, once a source of freedom and independence, became an impossible source of terror. Every person who walked toward her car on the street was a potential threat, someone acting suspiciously. Every time she was forced to follow GPS directions down an unfamiliar street, a feeling of being trapped, of losing her autonomy, would trigger a spike of panic. She began calling in sick, then refusing shifts, until finally, she had to quit. The loss of her job was a profound blow, reinforcing her feeling of helplessness. It also severed her from her daily routines and coworkers, deepening a sense of isolation that had already taken root. She felt set apart from her friends and family, as if she were living behind a pane of glass, watching their normal lives unfold while she was stuck replaying the worst moment of hers. To cope, she developed small, private rituals. Sometimes, she would just tell herself the event did not really happen, or that it wasn't that bad, a flimsy shield of magical thinking against the persistent memories. On harder nights, when the anxiety was a physical weight on her chest, she started smoking marijuana, finding that it was the only thing that could quiet the noise in her head long enough for her to fall asleep.

It was her sister finding her crying in her car in their parents' driveway—unable to bring herself to even be a passenger for a short trip to the store—that served as the final breaking point. Priya realized she had not only lost her car and her job that night; she was losing herself. She is now seeking help, terrified that this feeling of being broken and perpetually unsafe is permanent, but holding onto a desperate hope that she might one day feel like the person she was before the taillights disappeared into the dark.
